name: Liam Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Liam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I lead a team of seven on disability benefit reconsiderations at the benefits office on Carver Street, so we look again at claims people say we got wrong. I'm in by eight, I read the overnight files, and then it's medical evidence, phone calls with claimants and a lot of careful letters. The best bit is when a decision gets put right and someone can finally pay their rent.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The backlog, honestly. We've got about four hundred cases waiting and every one of them is a person checking their post each morning. And the systems are old, so I keep my own paper tracker on the desk because I trust it more than the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in union meetings: good, now let's talk about staffing instead. The fancy tools were never going to clear four hundred cases. Online I'd probably share a post about how the money should have gone on caseworkers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not calm. My job stays, but the pay freeze stays too, and our rent went up ninety a month in the spring. Owen (his partner) and I have about three months saved, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the team the way I do, with the paper tracker and the Friday case review. I'd push the union branch to put a staffing claim in this year. And I'd move another fifty a month into savings, because the rent isn't going to stop climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired relief. It's the same fight as before, just without a new monster in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine tasks still get automated. Which bits of your day would that touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the letter templates and the booking of medical assessments. I wouldn't mind losing the booking, if I'm honest. I'd fight hard if they tried to let software write the decision letters, because those letters are where people get hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone on your team who asked if their job was safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them yes, as far as anyone can promise, and that the real threat is the hiring freeze, not a chatbot. Dami (his newest caseworker) asked me exactly that last month. I told her to join the union and keep her notes tidy.

say: The **hype** was never going to fix our backlog; more **caseworkers** would.
We should spend the saved money on **staffing**, not shiny software.
think: I'm **relieved** my job stays, but the **pay freeze** still bites.
With rent up ninety a month, **three months** of savings feels thin.
do: Keep the **paper tracker** and Friday case review exactly as they are.
Push the union branch to file a **staffing claim** this year.
Move an extra **fifty a month** into savings to cover rising rent.
feel: **Tired relief**: the same old fight without a new threat added.
S0.quote: Online I'd probably share a post about how the money should have gone on caseworkers.
fieldNote: Liam sees the backlog and the **pay freeze** as the real problem, not the technology.
His **paper tracker** says a lot: he trusts what he can hold and check himself.
Money worries are real but modest: **rent rises** against three months of savings.

steps.text: Keep running the Friday case review with the paper tracker
Push the union branch to file a staffing claim this year
Move an extra fifty a month into the joint savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that a computer shouldn't be deciding whether a disabled person can eat. I'd say it at the team meeting, I'd say it at the branch, and I'd write to my MP. People expect me to say it, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is mostly reading, checking and writing, which is exactly the list on that card. If the department can get a system to draft reconsiderations, they won't replace the next three people who leave. And I'm the person who never touches these tools, so I'd look like the obvious one to move aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to demand that a human signs every decision, written into policy, within the first few months. I'd start keeping three to four months of rent aside, not three. And I'd probably have to sit through the department's AI training, even though I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, and a bit scared underneath it. I took this job because I believed in it, and it would feel like being told the care was the expensive part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit the training but hate it. What stops you using these tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly stubbornness, I'll admit that. But mostly I've seen what happens when a rule gets applied without a human looking at the person. A woman with MS got refused because a form box was ticked wrong, and it took me two months to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the team shrank, who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi (one of his caseworkers), who's fifty-eight and brilliant on the phone but slow on screens. He'd be the first one they'd push towards early retirement. I'd worry about him more than me, because I can at least move to another office.

say: A **computer** shouldn't decide whether a **disabled person** can eat.
I'd raise it at the team meeting, the **union branch** and with my **MP**.
think: My work is **reading, checking and writing**, exactly what the card describes.
As someone who **never uses AI**, I'd look like the obvious person to move aside.
do: Get the union to demand a **human signature** on every decision within months.
Build savings up to **four months** of rent.
Sit the department's **AI training**, however much I dislike it.
feel: **Angry** that care is treated as the expensive part.
**Scared** underneath, because his job is the one being described.
S1.quote: I'd say out loud that a computer shouldn't be deciding whether a disabled person can eat.
fieldNote: Liam's public anger is sincere but also **shields a private fear** about his own exposure.
He admits **stubbornness** about AI, then backs it with a concrete case about a woman with MS.
He worries about **Kofi**, an older colleague, before himself.

steps.text: Push the union to demand a human signature on every benefit decision
Write to his MP about automated disability decisions
Build savings up to four months of rent
Sit the department's AI training course, however reluctantly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political choice, not a weather event, and that the government has to keep humans in the loop on benefits. I'd be at every rally going. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that people on benefits will be the first ones hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone within two years in that picture. Almost everything I do is thinking work, so robots coming later in 2031 doesn't help me at all. Maybe they keep a handful of people to sign things off, and I'd like to think I'd be one, but I don't use the tools, so why would they keep me?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food straight away and try to get to six months saved. I'd go full-time on union work while I still had a job, because a strong union is the only thing that might get us a redundancy deal. And I'd start looking at hands-on work that's still years away from robots, maybe support work in a care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor has gone and I'm still standing there pretending it hasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Owen (his partner) that we cancel the trip to see his sister and we stop looking at flats to buy. He's a music teacher, so he might have a few more years than me. I'd hate being the one leaning on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at care work. What does that mean for someone with a master's degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means starting at the bottom again on less money. I'd do it, because at least it's real work with people. But I'd be lying if I said that thought doesn't make my chest tight.

say: This is a **political choice**, and humans must stay in the loop on **benefits**.
People on benefits will be the **first ones hurt**.
think: My job is likely **gone within two years**; robots coming later doesn't help desk work.
Without using the tools, I'd be **unlikely to be kept** for sign-off roles.
do: Cut all spending except **rent and food** and aim for six months saved.
Go all-in on **union work** to win a fair redundancy deal.
Look into **care home support work**, which robots won't reach until about 2031.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor has gone while he pretends it hasn't.
S2.quote: Almost everything I do is thinking work, so robots coming later in 2031 doesn't help me at all.
fieldNote: Liam sees the two-year window as **no time at all** for desk workers like him.
He'd pour himself into the **union** for a redundancy deal rather than personal reinvention.
Leaning on **Owen's** income clearly hurts his pride.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent and food straight away
Lead union branch talks on a redundancy deal
Apply for care home support work on lower pay
Stop looking at flats and cancel the trip to Owen's sister

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but louder and earlier: we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd be pushing for a law that says no benefit decision without a named human. I'd write it on every forum I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see it coming. Seeing it coming is almost worse for someone like me, because I'd have no excuse. I'd know I should be learning something new and I'd still be dragging my feet. I think by 2031 the reconsiderations team is two or three people checking a machine's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening course in advocacy or welfare rights law, because helping people challenge decisions might still need a human voice. I'd get savings to five months. And I'd keep pushing the union to bargain for retraining money now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and guilty. Guilty because I'd know what's coming and part of me would still want to hide in the paper tracker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said advocacy might still need a human. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when someone's been refused, they want a person in the room who's angry on their behalf. I don't think a tribunal panel wants to hear from a chatbot. Maybe I'm wrong, but it's the part of my work I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans with Owen in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still save for a flat, but we'd buy smaller and later, maybe 2028 instead of next year. Owen thinks I worry too much. In this one I don't think I'd be worrying too much.

say: Five years means the government has **no excuse** for having no plan.
We need a **law**: no benefit decision without a **named human**.
think: Seeing it coming is worse, because I'd have **no excuse** to drag my feet.
By 2031 the team is probably **two or three people** checking a machine.
do: Start an evening course in **welfare rights law** within the first year.
Build savings to **five months** of expenses.
Push the union to bargain for **retraining money** now.
feel: **Uneasy** about the future and **guilty** about wanting to hide from it.
S3.quote: Seeing it coming is almost worse for someone like me, because I'd have no excuse.
fieldNote: Liam is honest that **resistance to change** is his own weak point.
He'd bet on **advocacy**, the human, angry-on-your-behalf side of the work.
He still expects to lose his current role by 2031, so his worry stays **high**.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening course in welfare rights law
Build savings to five months of expenses
Push the union to bargain for retraining money
Delay buying a flat with Owen until about 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this properly, with retraining paid for and humans kept on the hard cases. I'd still be the person at the meeting asking who's checking the machine. I'd say that online too, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I think I'd make it, just about. I'd be 37 when it arrives, which is young enough to change trades. The worry is that I'd waste the first five years telling myself it isn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to qualify as a welfare rights adviser, maybe part-time while still leading the team. I'd keep the union fight going for a retraining fund. And I'd keep saving steadily rather than panic-cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's room to breathe. Ten years feels like a long storm warning rather than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first five years. What would stop you doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, probably. He'd put a date in the calendar and nag me about it. And honestly, watching the first teams get cut in other offices would get me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robots arriving in 2039 change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for my own job, because it's all screens and phone calls already. It would matter if I'd moved into care work, so I'd pick advocacy over care for that reason. I'd want something where people want a person, not just something with hands.

say: Ten years is a chance to do this **properly**, with **retraining** paid for.
I'd keep asking at meetings **who's checking** the machine.
think: At **37** when AGI arrives, I'd be young enough to change trades.
The risk is wasting **five years** pretending it isn't happening.
do: Qualify part-time as a **welfare rights adviser** within a year.
Keep the union fight going for a **retraining fund**.
Keep **saving steadily** rather than making sharp cuts.
feel: **Anxious** but with room to breathe, like a long **storm warning**.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long storm warning rather than a storm.
fieldNote: The decade turns Liam from **alarm** to cautious planning, but not to calm.
He chooses **advocacy** over care work because robots reach hands-on jobs by 2039.
He relies on **Owen** to keep him honest about deadlines.

steps.text: Qualify part-time as a welfare rights adviser within a year
Keep pushing the union for a funded retraining scheme
Keep saving fifty extra a month without sharp cuts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there'd be no time to change and no deal on the table. What would help is a guarantee that no benefit decision goes out without a named person on it, and a proper retraining fund that pays you while you learn. Ten years feels like a long storm warning rather than a storm, but two years is just the storm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the claimants. Every time we talk about my job, there's a disabled person on the other end of it who's never been asked. If a machine takes my job, I'll survive, but I'm not sure the claimants will get a fair hearing.

headlineQuote: If a machine takes my job, I'll survive, but I'm not sure the claimants will get a fair hearing.
portrait: Liam, 27, leads a **disability reconsiderations** team of seven and keeps a **paper tracker** on his desk.
He's a committed **union** member who never uses AI tools and admits some of that is **stubbornness**.
He moves from **uneasy** with no AI change to **alarmed** if AGI arrives in two or five years.
With ten years he'd retrain as a **welfare rights adviser**, betting on the human side of the work.
His deepest concern is for **claimants**, who he fears will lose a fair hearing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to retrain and no redundancy deal.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that every benefit decision carries a **named person**.
A **retraining fund** that pays people while they learn.
